outcome: No source found reports a proof, a counterexample, or a bound that settles or moves the question of whether each base b >= 2 has infinitely many palindromic primes; the question is still stated as open in the most recent sources read (Chourasiya-Johnston v5, Nov 2025; Johnston-Kerr v1, Jan 2026), and the 2024-2026 activity found concerns neighbouring questions (square-free or cube-free palindromes, reversed primes) that do not give palindromic primes.
problem_asks: (1) For each integer base b >= 2, are there infinitely many palindromic primes, meaning primes whose base-b digit string reads the same forwards and backwards? (2) The bullet asks this 'to every base': a positive answer needs infinitely many base-b palindromic primes for all b >= 2 at once, and a finite count in any single base would answer it negatively. Wikipedia singles out base 10 ('not known if there are infinitely many palindromic primes in base 10'), but the frozen bullet is about every base. The statement asks for existence of infinitely many, not for bounds or counts.

events.what_happened: William D. Banks, Derrick N. Hart and Mayumi Sakata, 'Almost all palindromes are composite' (arXiv:math/0405056; Math. Res. Lett. 11 (2004) 853-868). They study palindromes in a fixed base g >= 2 over congruence classes and derive a nontrivial upper bound on the number of prime palindromes n <= x as x tends to infinity, hence that almost all palindromes are composite. The arXiv abstract gives no explicit formula; I did not open the full PDF.
events.revisions: v1 only (submitted 4 May 2004). Journal reference Math. Res. Lett. 11 (2004) 853-868 is taken from a citing reference in search results, not from the arXiv page, which lists no journal reference.
events.delivers: An upper bound, in every base, on the number of base-b palindromic primes up to x, showing they are sparse among palindromes. No lower bound and no statement of infinitude in any base.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: infinitude for every base b >= 2 is untouched.

checked_by.who: Mathematical Research Letters (journal of record for the published version)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in vol. 11 (2004), per a citing reference; the journal page was not opened and I did not confirm the acceptance process directly
checked_by.where: https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0405056 (no journal reference on this page; MRL citation from search results only)

events.direction: Cuts toward sparsity of palindromic primes. It neither asserts nor refutes infinitude.

events.what_happened: Sylvain Col, a paper on palindromes in arithmetic progressions (French title 'Palindromes dans les progressions arithmetiques', Acta Arith. 137 (2009) 1-41, per a 2011 citing paper seen in search results; Wikipedia cites 'Col, 2006'). Per Dartyge et al. (arXiv:2309.11380, introduction, section 1.1), Col 'has obtained an upper bound of the right order of magnitude for the number of palindromic primes in every base b >= 2': the number of prime palindromes below x in base b is O_b(number of palindromes below x / log x). I did not open Col's paper, so this rests on the citing text.
events.revisions: Two dates appear in secondary sources: 2006 (Wikipedia citation) and 2009 (Acta Arithmetica volume). The first public written form is not resolved, so the year given is the earliest seen and is uncertain.
events.delivers: An upper bound of the right order, in every base, on the count of base-b palindromic primes up to x (relative to the count of palindromes). No lower bound and no infinitude.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The bound gives sparsity, not existence.
events.time_since_posted: about 17 to 20 years (2006 or 2009 to October 2026)
events.doubts: The statement is secondhand and Col's own text was not read. The constant depends on the base, and the exact form of the bound is only as quoted by Dartyge et al.
events.direction: Cuts toward sparsity. It neither asserts nor refutes infinitude.

events.what_happened: Aleksandr Tuxanidy and Daniel Panario, 'Infinitude of palindromic almost-prime numbers' (arXiv:2307.16637). They prove that in any base there are infinitely many palindromes with at most six prime divisors, each relatively large. In section 1.2 they state Conjecture 1.1: 'for any base b >= 2, there are infinitely many prime numbers that are b-palindromic', calling it 'perhaps one of the most difficult unsolved problems'. The abstract page alone does not show the conjecture; I read it in the v3 HTML.
events.revisions: v1 31 Jul 2023; v2 16 Nov 2023; v3 23 Jul 2024 (the version I read).
events.delivers: Infinitely many palindromes (not primes) in every base, each with at most six prime divisors, each relatively large. No palindromic prime is produced. 'Relatively large' is not made precise in the abstract.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The result concerns palindromes with few prime factors. The conjecture itself is stated, not proved.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 years 2 months. Later papers use its equidistribution estimate as an input (Johnston-Kerr 2026, from the arXiv abstract page), but none reviews the result as such.
events.direction: Cuts neither way on the conjecture. It proves a weaker statement about palindromes and restates the palindromic-prime conjecture as open.

events.what_happened: Cecile Dartyge, Bruno Martin, Joel Rivat, Igor E. Shparlinski and Cathy Swaenepoel, 'Reversible primes' (arXiv:2309.11380), in base 2. A sieve bound on how often a prime and its binary reversal are both prime; asymptotic counts of n-bit integers and their reversals that are squarefree or have at most 8 prime factors. Section 1.1 says that 'unlike reversible primes, the distribution of palindromic primes has already been deeply investigated' and records Col's bound (see col-palindromic-prime-bound).
events.delivers: Binary reversible primes (primes whose binary reverse is prime): a sieve-type upper bound and counting results. Nothing about palindromic primes, and no claim of infinitude of reversible or palindromic primes in any base. The paper states, for squarefree palindromes, 'it is not known whether there exists infinitely many squarefree palindromes' (quoted via the HTML extraction).
events.remains: All of problem_asks. Reversible primes are a different object from palindromic primes.

checked_by.who: Journal of the London Mathematical Society (DOI 10.1112/jlms.12883, listed on the arXiv page)
checked_by.what_they_did: Listed as the journal version. Not verified: the journal page was not opened.

events.direction: Does not bear on the palindromic-prime conjecture. It concerns a different object (reversal, not palindrome).

events.what_happened: Hirotaka Kobayashi, Yuta Suzuki and Ryota Umezawa, 'Counting relatively prime pairs of palindromes' (arXiv:2311.15002). Asymptotic count of coprime pairs of palindromes of a fixed odd length in any base g >= 2, answering a problem of Banks and Shparlinski (2005). Per a search snippet, the paper notes that every even-length palindrome is divisible by g+1, which is why it restricts to odd length. I did not verify that sentence in the paper.
events.delivers: A count of coprime palindrome pairs of odd length. It says nothing about primes.
events.direction: Does not bear on the conjecture. It is about coprime palindrome pairs, not prime palindromes.

events.what_happened: Gautami Bhowmik and Yuta Suzuki, 'On Telhcirid's theorem on arithmetic progressions' (arXiv:2406.13334). Studies reversed primes (digit reversals of primes), not palindromic primes. Proves that reversed primes occur in any arithmetic progression meeting the basic necessary conditions, provided the base is sufficiently large, with an effective Siegel-Walfisz type result.
events.delivers: Reversed primes in arithmetic progressions for large bases. Nothing about palindromes or palindromic primes.
events.direction: Does not bear on the conjecture. Reversed primes are a different object.

events.what_happened: Shashi Chourasiya and Daniel R. Johnston, 'Power-free palindromes and reversed primes' (arXiv:2503.21136). Results: for bases b >= 26000 there are infinitely many primes p whose reversal is square-free; for every base b >= 2 there are infinitely many cube-free palindromes (v5); asymptotic counts. In the introduction they state Conjecture 1.2: 'For every base b>=2, there are infinitely many palindromic primes', and say 'Currently, both of these conjectures appear out of reach, particularly Conjecture 1.2 which would imply Conjecture 1.1' (Conjecture 1.1 is the reversible-primes conjecture). I read these sentences in the v5 HTML. Whether v1 contains Conjecture 1.2 was not checked.
events.revisions: v1 27 Mar 2025; v2 15 Apr 2025; v3 8 Oct 2025; v4 25 Oct 2025; v5 20 Nov 2025 ('minor corrections to Theorem 1.5 and Lemma 2.1'). The v1 abstract, as read, says palindromes are 4th-power-free; v5 says cube-free. This is version drift in the palindrome result, not in the conjecture.
events.delivers: Nothing toward palindromic primes. It restates Conjecture 1.2 as open. Its theorems concern square-free reversals of primes (b >= 26000) and cube-free palindromes in every base, neither of which is a palindromic prime.
events.time_since_posted: about 18 months. No public review found; the paper is self-described as relying on a computational argument with code in a GitHub repository (not opened).
events.doubts: Version drift between v1 (4th-power-free palindromes) and v5 (cube-free palindromes), with Theorem 1.5 corrected in v5. The authors' own statement that Conjecture 1.2 'appear[s] out of reach' is a status statement, not a doubt about any result.
events.direction: Neutral on the conjecture. The authors treat it as open and prove neighbouring results.

events.what_happened: Cecile Dartyge, Joel Rivat and Cathy Swaenepoel, 'Prime numbers with an almost prime reverse' (arXiv:2506.21642). For base b, shows that for at least c_b b^lambda lambda^(-2) primes p in [b^(lambda-1), b^lambda - 1], the reverse of p has at most Omega_b prime factors.
events.revisions: v1 25 Jun 2025; v2 10 Jul 2025 ('minor corrections and page settings modified').
events.delivers: Reversed primes (reverse of a prime has few factors). Nothing about palindromes or palindromic primes.
events.direction: Does not bear on the conjecture. Reversed primes are a different object.

events.what_happened: Daniel Johnston, talk 'Recent progress on emirps and palindromic primes', Linfoot Number Theory Seminar, UNSW, 9 July 2025 (seminar abstract as read on the Bristol page). The abstract says: 'In every base, it has long been conjectured that there are infinitely many emirps and palindromic primes', that newer analytic techniques are producing 'a flurry of recent papers', and that 'upcoming work from various authors [is] coming soon to an arXiv near you'. It states no new result.
events.delivers: Nothing. It restates the conjecture and advertises forthcoming work.

events.what_happened: Gautami Bhowmik and Yuta Suzuki, 'The Zsiflaw-Legeis theorem for arbitrary bases' (arXiv:2507.08714). Analogues of the Dirichlet and Siegel-Walfisz theorems for reversed primes (digit reversals of primes) in arbitrary bases, extending their 2024 large-base result.
events.delivers: Reversed primes in arithmetic progressions for all bases. Nothing about palindromic primes.
events.direction: Does not bear on the conjecture. Reversed primes are a different object.

events.what_happened: Daniel R. Johnston and Bryce Kerr, 'The infinitude of square-free palindromes' (arXiv:2601.07097, math.NT). For any fixed base b >= 2 there are infinitely many square-free palindromes in base b, with an asymptotic count. It resolves a problem of Shparlinski (Problem 58 in his list of Problems on Exponential and Character Sums, per the paper's introduction). The introduction says the result 'can be viewed as an approximation of the conjecture that there exists infinitely many palindromes which are also prime numbers', and that 'a proof of this conjecture still remains firmly out of reach'. Read in the v1 HTML and the abstract page.
events.revisions: v1 11 Jan 2026; v2 20 Jan 2026 (current). 24 pages, 1 figure.
events.delivers: Infinitely many square-free palindromes in every base b >= 2 (not prime), with an asymptotic count. It does not produce a single palindromic prime. The authors say it approximates, but does not give, the palindromic-prime statement.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: no palindromic prime is produced in any base.
events.time_since_posted: about 9 months. The only later items found build on it (Tuxanidy 2026 square-free distribution, from search results); no referee report or verification found.
events.direction: Neutral on the conjecture. It is a positive result about a different object (square-free palindromes, not primes), which the authors say approximates the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Aleksandr Tuxanidy, 'Distribution of square-free palindromes' (arXiv:2603.02549). Establishes an exponent of distribution 1/16 for square-free palindromes, building on the Johnston-Kerr result (per search results; the abstract page does not name it).
events.delivers: A distribution result for square-free palindromes. Not primes. The abstract page says its only subject is square-free palindromes and does not mention palindromic primes.
events.direction: Does not bear on the conjecture. It concerns square-free palindromes.

events.what_happened: Michael Harm and Daniel R. Johnston, 'The reverse Goldbach problem and a refined Zsiflaw-Legeis theorem' (arXiv:2605.21876). Results on reversed primes, including that every large odd integer is the sum of a prime and two reversed primes. The page does not mention palindromic primes or emirps by name.
events.delivers: Additive results on reversed primes. Nothing about palindromic primes.
events.direction: Does not bear on the conjecture. Reversed primes are a different object.

It names no paper, researcher or pattern. Its only primary-looking link is a YouTube video, which I did not open. Two dedicated searches found no DeepMind blog post, paper or established science-news coverage of such a result.

events.doubts: The only source is a headline and video description on an aggregator site. No primary source was found. The 'AI' attribution rests on the headline alone.
events.direction: Unknown. If the pattern concerns primes in general, it does not bear on palindromic primes.

summary: No source found reports a proof, counterexample or bound that settles or moves the existence question for palindromic primes in any base since 26 January 2024. The problem's status is set out in three sources, read in the sections that matter. Tuxanidy and Panario (arXiv:2307.16637, 2023) state the base-b conjecture as Conjecture 1.1 and call it 'perhaps one of the most difficult unsolved problems' (v3 HTML, section 1.2). Chourasiya and Johnston (arXiv:2503.21136 v5, Nov 2025) restate it as Conjecture 1.2 and say it 'appear[s] out of reach' (v5 HTML). Johnston and Kerr (arXiv:2601.07097, Jan 2026) say a proof 'still remains firmly out of reach' (v1 HTML, introduction). The Wikipedia article (last edited 17 August 2026, opened) says only that 'it is not known if there are infinitely many palindromic primes in base 10' and makes no statement for every base. The 2024-2026 activity is on neighbouring questions. Johnston-Kerr proves infinitely many square-free palindromes in every base, and the authors say this approximates but does not give the palindromic-prime statement. Chourasiya-Johnston prove cube-free palindromes and square-free reversals of primes. The reversed-prime papers (Bhowmik-Suzuki 2024 and 2025, Dartyge-Rivat-Swaenepoel 2025, Harm-Johnston 2026) concern reversals, not palindromes. I recorded these as discounted events, with reasons, because they answer different questions. Close calls: (i) the counting bounds, Banks-Hart-Sakata (2004) and Col (cited by Dartyge et al. as an upper bound of the right order, in every base), bound the number of palindromic primes up to x. That is the natural quantity the problem is about, but both predate the window and point to sparsity, not existence. Col's paper was not opened, so its date and exact form are secondhand. (ii) Johnston-Kerr's asymptotic counts square-free palindromes, not primes, so I did not treat it as moving the prime count. Arithmetic check (my own, not from a source): an even-length palindrome in base g is divisible by g+1, so the only even-length palindromic prime a base can have is g+1 itself when that is prime (11 in base 10). This is consistent with the Wikipedia and OEIS A002385 notes. Searches also surfaced a conflict on Tuxanidy-Panario's conjecture: a search snippet said the paper 'states the same base-b palindromic prime conjecture', and I confirmed that in the full v3 HTML, so the snippet was right. AI involvement: none of the palindromic-prime sources names an AI system. Chourasiya-Johnston's computations are code, which is computer assistance rather than AI. The only AI-attributed claim near the problem is the June 2026 Lifeboat headline ('Google DeepMind AI Discovered a Mathematical Pattern Hidden in Prime Numbers'). I could not trace it to any paper, it names no pattern, and it does not mention palindromes, so it is recorded as unverified. Two AI-math papers surfaced by the searches do not mention palindromic primes. Le Duc and Liberti (arXiv:2510.12829, read in full) test 66 conjectures on primes and cyclic numbers with gpt-5 agents ('Both agents are gpt-5 LLMs that have access to a Python interpreter'). AlphaEvolve (arXiv:2511.02864) shows no palindromic-prime content in the roughly two-thirds of its HTML that I could read; that HTML is truncated. Both are out of scope for this problem and are noted here only so the later pass knows they were checked. In passing: the Wikipedia infobox gives a 'largest known' palindromic prime of 10^1888529 - 10^944264 - 1 (found 18 October 2021), which conflicts with the 474,501-digit figure in other sources. I did not research this.
competing_reading: One could count the 2004 and c. 2006 upper bounds (Banks-Hart-Sakata; Col), and Johnston-Kerr's square-free count, as a bound on a quantity the problem is about, and so as an event that moved it. The palindromic-prime count up to x is the natural quantity, and all three results are about how many palindromes survive a restriction. On that reading the record contains a bearing event, which is evidence of sparsity. The reply is that the upper bounds show palindromic primes are rare, not that there are infinitely many, and they predate the window; Johnston-Kerr counts square-free palindromes, not primes. Neither changes what the bullet asks, but the judging pass should see both readings.
what_would_settle_it: A preprint or paper showing that for some or every base b >= 2 there are infinitely many b-palindromic primes, or that some base has finitely many. To confirm that nothing else happened, a direct arXiv listing or full-text search for 'palindromic prime', 'primendrome' (the term Johnston and Kerr suggest in a footnote), 'b-palindromic' and 'emirp' with palindrome terms, limited to January 2024 to October 2026. I could not run that directly, and only the general web search tool was used. Also useful: Col's paper (its date and exact bound), the rest of the AlphaEvolve HTML, and a primary DeepMind source for the June 2026 headline.

events.credibility_reason: Only an aggregator headline over a video description; it names no paper, researcher or pattern, no primary source could be traced, and it does not concern palindromic primes.

judgement.why: The statement asks whether every base has infinitely many palindromic primes. No event produces a palindromic prime family or a finiteness result. The Banks-Hart-Sakata and Col upper bounds count palindromic primes up to x but say nothing toward infinitude or finiteness; an upper bound on a count that could still be infinite does not move the yes/no question, so I scored them none rather than bound (they are pre-snapshot either way). Almost-prime, square-free and cube-free palindromes, coprime palindrome pairs and reversed/reversible primes are all changed questions, so variant. The seminar talk and the Lifeboat headline deliver nothing; the latter is also set aside as not credible and has no AI system with a quote, so ai_role none. No AI contributed mathematics to any event.
judgement.doubts: Col's date (2006 vs 2009) is unresolved but is before 2024 either way. The journal acceptances used for digested (MRL, Acta Arith., JLMS) come from citing references and arXiv metadata rather than opened journal pages; this affects no outcome. arXiv full-text search was not run directly, so a missed 2024-2026 preprint is possible.
